source_text:
Ἄμεινόν ἐστιν σιωπᾶν καὶ εἶναι, ἦ λαλοῦντα μὴ εἶναι. καλὸν τὸ διδάσκειν, ἐὰν ὁ λέγων ποιῇ. εἶς οὖν διδάσκαλος, ὃς εἶπεν, καὶ ἐγένετο: καὶ ἃ σιγῶν δὲ πεποίηκεν ἄξια τοῦ πατρός ἐστιν.
ὁ λόγον Ἰησοῦ κεκτημένος ἀληθῶς δύναται καὶ τῆς ἡσυχίας αὐτοῦ ἀκούειν, ἵνα τέλειος ᾖ, ἵνα δἰ ὦν λαλεῖ πράσσῃ καὶ δἰ ὦν σιγᾷ γινώσκηται.
οὐδὲν λανθάνει τὸν κύριον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰ κρυπτὰ ἡμῶν ἐγγὺς αὐτῷ ἐστιν. πάντα οὖν ποιῶμεν ὡς αὐτοῦ ἐν ἡμῖν κατοικοῦντος, ἵνα ὦμεν αὐτοῦ ναοὶ καὶ αὐτὸς ἐν ἡμῖν θεὸς ἡμῶν: ὅπερ καὶ ἔστιν καὶ φανήσεται πρὸ προσώπου ἡμῶν, ἐξ ὦν δικαίως ἀγαπῶμεν αὐτόν.
thought_title: Silence and action reveal the true disciple
orientation: Ignatius is writing to the Ephesians, urging them to be true disciples whose deeds match their words, because God dwells in them.
pass_a_gloss: It is better to be silent and to be, than speaking not to be. It is good to teach, if the one who speaks also does. There is one teacher, who spoke, and it came to be: and the things which he did while silent are worthy of the Father. The one who truly possesses the word of Jesus is able also to hear his silence, in order that he may be perfect, in order that through the things he speaks he may act and through the things he is silent about he may be known. Nothing escapes the Lord, but even our hidden things are near to him. Therefore let us do all things as if he dwells in us, in order that we may be his temples and he in us our God: which indeed also is and will appear before our face, from the things by which we rightly love him.

choices.english: to be silent and to be
choices.why: Keeps the stark contrast between silence and being, matching the Greek infinitive pair exactly
rejected: to keep silence and be real

choices.english: the one who truly possesses the word of Jesus
choices.why: Renders κεκτημένος as 'possesses' to convey acquired, held possession, and keeps 'word of Jesus' as the object
rejected: he who has the word of Jesus

choices.why: Literal rendering of the paradox of hearing silence, which is the point of the passage

choices.english: as if he dwells in us
choices.why: Keeps the participial construction with 'as if' to preserve the conditional force of the indwelling
Literal rendering of the Semitic idiom, preserving the biblical flavor

bible_refs.note: εἶπεν, καὶ ἐγένετο (he spoke, and it came to be)

pass_b_english: It is better to be silent and to be, than to speak and not be. Teaching is good, if the one who speaks also does. There is one teacher, who spoke and it came to be; and the things he has done in silence are worthy of the Father.
The one who truly possesses the word of Jesus is able to hear even his silence, so that he may be perfect, so that through what he speaks he acts, and through what he is silent about he is known.

Nothing escapes the Lord's notice; even our hidden things are near to him. Let us therefore do everything as if he dwells in us, so that we may be his temples and he may be in us as our God. This is indeed the case, and it will appear before our face, because of which we rightly love him.

problems.why: The citation Psalm 33:9 does not match; LXX Psalm 32:9 / Hebrew Psalm 33:9 has 'αὐτὸς εἶπεν καὶ ἐγενήθησαν,' but Ignatius's 'καὶ ἐγένετο' more closely echoes Genesis 1 (LXX 'καὶ ἐγένετο'/'καὶ ἐγένετο οὕτως'). The brief requires standard English Bible book names and Hebrew Psalm numbering; this is not a Psalm quotation.
problems.fix: Genesis 1 (or remove the citation if uncertain).

problems.why: ἐξ ὦν means 'from which things' or 'on the basis of which,' not 'because.' The Greek indicates the manifestation results from the grounds/conditions by which we love him rightly, not causal 'because.'
problems.fix: from which things we love him rightly, or: by which we rightly love him.

by which we rightly love him.

problems.quote: This is indeed the case, and it will appear before our face, by which we rightly love him.
problems.why: The sentence is syntactically broken; 'by which' has no clear antecedent.
problems.fix: Rewrite: 'This is indeed the case, and it will appear before us, and because of it we rightly love him.'

edits.old: This is indeed the case, and it will appear before our face, by which we rightly love him.

fixed: The source reads 'ἐξ ὦν δικαίως ἀγαπῶμεν αὐτόν' — 'from the things by which we rightly love him.' The English 'by which we rightly love him' is a literal rendering but the antecedent is unclear. The phrase 'ἐξ ὦν' means 'from which things' or 'because of which,' referring to the preceding statement about God dwelling in us and appearing before us. Changing to 'because of which' clarifies the causal relationship while staying close to the source.

problems.quote: There is, then, one teacher, who spoke and it came to be (Psalm LXX 32:9 (33:9))
problems.why: Psalm 33:9 (LXX 32:9) says 'He spoke, and it came to be'—but 'one teacher' is Ignatius's gloss, not in Psalm.
problems.fix: Cite as allusion, not direct quote; or note adaptation.

problems.why: Sentence structure is garbled; 'There is, then, one teacher' reads like word-for-word gloss.
problems.fix: Rephrase: 'There is one teacher who spoke and it came to be.'

problems.why: Reference format is confusing; reader may not know which Psalm number to look up.

fixed: Removed 'then' and simplified the sentence structure; the source has 'εἶς οὖν διδάσκαλος' (one teacher, then), but the English 'There is, then, one teacher' is awkward and the 'then' is not essential to the meaning.

Changed the Psalm reference to the modern numbering 'Psalm 33:9' per the brief's instruction to use standard English Bible book names and modern numbering; the LXX numbering is not needed in the text.

The earlier edit to 'because of which we rightly love him' was correct and is retained; the source 'ἐξ ὦν δικαίως ἀγαπῶμεν αὐτόν' means 'from the things by which we rightly love him', and the English 'because of which' captures this adequately.

last_rejected.fix: and from these things we rightly love him
last_rejected.ruling: ἐξ ὦν = 'from which things'; 'by which' reasonably conveys causal basis. Meaning preserved; not a major error.
